# Tomography {#sec-tomography}

The tomography stage is found in `backend/core/simulator/tomography.py`. It is
an alternative to the exact simulator. Instead of computing the state, the three
Pauli expectations of each qubit are **measured** on the backend. The effect of
the real noise is therefore seen.

The tomography is selected with `strategy="tomography"` in `compile`.

## Why the state is measured, and not computed {.unnumbered}

The exact simulator gives the ideal state. It cannot show the error of the real
device. The tomography is used when the effect of the noise is of interest. The
measured result can be compared with the ideal result, and the difference is the
error of the device. The exact statevector is therefore kept as the reference.

## `measure(native, backend, info, *, shots=1024, allow_paid=False)` {.unnumbered}

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `native` | `NativeCircuit` | required | The circuit to measure. |
| `backend` | any object | required | The backend that is used for the measurement. |
| `info` | `BackendInfo` | required | The backend information. The hardware flag is checked. |
| `shots` | int | `1024` | The number of shots for each circuit. |
| `allow_paid` | bool | `False` | It must be `True` before a paid backend is used. |

**Returns** a `SimulatedCircuit`, so that the rest of the pipeline is unchanged.

**Raises** `QVizError` when the backend is classified as hardware and
`allow_paid` is `False`. The guard is deliberately conservative: it is not
possible to know from the code whether the chosen backend spends credits, so the
safe default is to ask for confirmation. When the backend is free, the simple
fix is to pass `allow_paid=True`.

## Why the circuit is cut into prefixes {.unnumbered}

The state after every gate must be shown, not only the final state. A backend
can only be measured, so it cannot be asked for the state after gate `k` of a
long circuit.

The solution is to build a **prefix circuit** for every `k`. A prefix contains
the first `k` operations, and it is measured. In this way, the state after each
operation is obtained, one measurement at a time.

A prefix is built with `to_qiskit(native, upto=k)` (see the [`to_qiskit`
page](to-qiskit.qmd)). The first operations are the
same as in the full circuit, so the measured state is the state that the full
circuit would have at that point.

## Why three bases are needed {.unnumbered}

A single measurement in the Z basis gives only one number, the expectation
`⟨Z⟩`. The other two components of the Bloch vector are not visible in that
basis.

A rotation before the measurement is used to bring another axis into the Z
basis. Three cases are needed.

| Basis | Preparation before the measurement | What is measured |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Z | nothing | `⟨Z⟩` |
| X | a Hadamard gate on every qubit | `⟨X⟩` |
| Y | an `Sdg` gate, then a Hadamard, on every qubit | `⟨Y⟩` |

The reason for the rotations is the following. A Hadamard gate maps the `x` axis
onto the `z` axis, because `H Z H = X`. An `Sdg` followed by a Hadamard maps the
`y` axis onto the `z` axis. The three expectations `(x, y, z)` fully describe the
reduced state of one qubit.

## Why all the circuits are placed in one call {.unnumbered}

The number of circuits is `3 * N`, where `N` is the number of native operations.
On IonQ, only **one** job is allowed per run. All the circuits are therefore
placed in a single call to `backend.run(list_of_circuits, shots=shots)`. A
second call would stop the run with the message "only one job is allowed".

For a backend that is not IonQ, the circuits are transpiled for that backend
before they are sent. No job limit applies to the local simulators, but the same
single call is used everywhere, so that the code is the same for every backend.

A warning is logged, because the run time grows with `shots * 3 * N` on a noisy
simulator.

## How an expectation is found {.unnumbered}

The counts of a measurement are used. For one qubit `q`, the bit of the qubit is
read from each bitstring. The rightmost character is qubit 0, as everywhere in
the project.

$$
\langle \sigma \rangle_q = \frac{n_0 - n_1}{\text{shots}}
$$

where `n_0` and `n_1` are the numbers of shots in which the bit of qubit `q` is
0 or 1. The counts are marginalised, so the other qubits do not matter.

The three expectations give `x`, `y` and `z`. The vector is clipped to the unit
ball, and the angles are computed in the same way as in the exact simulator, so
that the output has the same shape.

## Known limitations and conflicts {.unnumbered}

- On IonQ, the remote strategy of the transpiler would also spend the single
  job. The transpiler is therefore called with `allow_remote=False` when the
  tomography is used, and the local transpile strategy is taken.
- On a backend that is not IonQ, the native gates have to be transpiled by Qiskit,
  which needs `qiskit-ionq` 1.0.3 or newer (the older versions give the gates no
  definition). With an older version a `TranspilationError` that says so is raised.
  On IonQ the circuits are sent as they are, and the version does not matter.
- The tomography is statistical. The error on each component is about
  `1 / sqrt(shots)`. A larger number of shots gives a better estimate.
- The number of circuits grows quickly. For a circuit with many gates, the run
  time and the cost grow with `3 * N`.
- On a backend that spends credits, `allow_paid=True` is required. This is a
  deliberate guard, and it may be relaxed when the backend is known to be free.
